extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, comparative politics, and civic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the social, religious, legal, and educational conditions that promote the maintenance and durability of a democratic republic, as argued in a classical political-theory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a foremost political institution
rubrics_metrics.description: “Religion in America takes no direct part in the government of society, but it must nevertheless be regarded as the foremost of the political institutions of that country; for if it does not impart a taste for freedom, it facilitates the use of free institutions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that religion extends beyond manners to the intelligence of the people; Americans view religious belief as indispensable to maintaining republican institutions. Provides examples (public attitudes, civic missions to western states) showing religion supports republican stability even when not wielding formal political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of Church and State (care taken to separate clergy from civil office)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Care taken by the Americans to separate the Church from the State—The laws, public opinion, and even the exertions of the clergy concur to promote this end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details legal exclusions (state constitutions barring ministers from civil or military office), public opinion, and clergy self-restraint. Argues clergy abstention from political office preserves religion’s moral authority and makes its influence more durable than when allied with state power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion should avoid alliance with political power
rubrics_metrics.description: “When a religion contracts an alliance of this nature [with government], I do not hesitate to affirm that it commits the same error... it risks that authority which is rightfully its own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that tying religion to temporal power forces it to adopt partisan maxims, reduces universality, and makes it vulnerable to the rise and fall of political regimes. Emphasizes long-term durability of religion when independent of state alliances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a moral check on political innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion lays down certain primal and immutable principles which check the human mind: 'Before it can perpetrate innovation, certain primal and immutable principles are laid down, and the boldest conceptions of human device are subjected to certain forms which retard and stop their completion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that religiously rooted moral restraints make citizens more circumspect, limit rash or unjust actions, and thereby favor tranquillity and the durability of political institutions. Illustrative anecdotes (judge rejecting witness who disbelieved in God) show public trust tied to religious norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display of faith and social reinforcement of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Americans combine the notions of Christianity and of liberty so intimately in their minds... they hold it to be indispensable to the maintenance of republican institutions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a social equilibrium where believers openly avow faith while unbelievers tend to conceal doubt; public opinion thus sustains religious observance. This social signaling reinforces religion’s civic role even when private belief varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education: universal elementary civic and religious instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: “In New England, every citizen receives the elementary notions of human knowledge; he is moreover taught the doctrines and the evidences of his religion, the history of his country, and the leading features of its Constitution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims broad elementary instruction (including religious and civic content) produces an enlightened populace capable of participating in republican government; contrasts rarity of wholly uninstructed persons in the U.S. with Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experience in self-government outweighs book-learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “The American learns to know the laws by participating in the act of legislation; and he takes a lesson in the forms of government from governing... True information is mainly derived from experience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that civic habits formed by participation (elections, local offices, legislation) produce competent citizens; warns that mere literacy without practical experience is insufficient to make citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid diffusion of public opinion and information
rubrics_metrics.description: “Rapidity with which opinions are diffused even in the uncultivated States of the West.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes infrastructural and communicative mechanisms (mail posts, newspapers reaching frontier settlers) that circulate opinions and civic norms broadly and quickly, reinforcing uniform civic habits across dispersed populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners and habits contribute more than laws; laws more than physical circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter claim: 'The Laws Contribute More To The Maintenance Of The Democratic Republic In The United States Than The Physical Circumstances Of The Country, And The Manners More Than The Laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts a hierarchy of causes for democratic stability: manners/habits (customs, civic culture) are the most important, then laws and institutions, then physical/geographic circumstances. The text advances this as a guiding analytic standard for assessing why democratic institutions endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great dangers to religion (and thus to its civic role): schism and indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: “The two great dangers which threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how schism causes competing fervor but preserves religious vitality, while indifference (lukewarmness, loss of conviction without replacement) leads to gradual decline; links indifference to political entanglement and to social conditions where religion is treated as partisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious sentiment rooted in human nature (religion as form of hope)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Religion, then, is simply another form of hope... Men cannot abandon their religious faith without a kind of aberration of intellect...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents a psychological/anthropological basis for religion’s persistence: as a natural human need it supplies hope and consolation, thereby underpinning its social durability even amid political change.
